newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: COMMONWEALTH GAMES-MALAYSIA SPARE NO EFFORT TO ENSURE MEMORABLE GAMES.
newsitem.headline: COMMONWEALTH GAMES-MALAYSIA SPARE NO EFFORT TO ENSURE MEMORABLE GAMES.

text.p: Six thousand athletes and officials. Seventy participating countries. A bill of more than $500 million. And one ex-general calling the shots.

Since outbidding the Australian city of Adelaide five years to host the 1998 Commonwealth Games, Kuala Lumpur has spared little effort or money for an event which has been granted importance equal to any of its domestic or foreign policies.

"This will be the last Commonwealth Games for this century and we want it to be the best," said Hashim Mohamed Ali, a former general and executive chairman of the local organising committee Sukom '98.
"I think there's a lot at stake here, including national pride," added Rustam Sani, a local political commentator. "Malaysia has always been interested in hosting Games of this kind."

With a budget of more than one billion ringgit ($400 million), the government is building the main Games village, a 100,000-capacity athletics stadium, a gymnastics stadium seating 16,000, a 12,000-capacity hockey stadium, a netball stadium for 4,000 people and a swimming arena seating 4,000 people.

Two multi-billion-dollar projects, a new international airport and an elevated rail network covering much of Kuala Lumpur, are expected to be completed before the Games, scheduled for September 11-21.
Corporations are pumping millions of dollars into new hotels and tourist attractions to house and pamper the thousands of spectators and visitors expected during the 10 days of the Games.
Hashim, 61, had retired when his brother-in-law, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, asked him five years ago to run the Games.
After travelling thousands of kilometres to see how other international sports meeting were organised, Hashim said he was confident of doing a good job in 1998.
"But in terms of planning, we still have plenty to do," he said.

The Games will feature 15 different events, six more than the 1994 Games in Victoria, Canada. These will be athletics, swimming, squash, men's and women's hockey, gymnastics, rugby union, cycling, badminton, boxing, shooting, lawn bowling, 10-pin bowling, weightlifting and cricket.
"We have good experience in badminton, cricket and hockey, but things like lawn bowling we are not used to, and there could be problems," said Hashim.
He is also concerned about getting the right technology "to avoid the slow results system they had at Atlanta (Olympics) and the mess created by the parking system there".
One of Hashim's main worries will be keeping to a 310 million ringgit ($124 million) budget for the Games.
"This budget is our own and will be in cash and kind," said Hashim. "The government has already spent on the infrastructure and we don't want to ask for more."
Sports Minister Muhyiddin Yassin said recently that money had to be spent for the Games "but there should be no waste".
His remarks preceded an attack from outspoken Australian Commonwealth Games Association secretary Arthur Tunstall, who accused Kuala Lumpur of buying the Games.
Malaysian officials rejected Tunsatall's allegations, saying the country had been chosen because the Commonwealth Games Federation (CFG) wanted a developing nation to host the Games.

"The last time the Commonwealth Games was hosted by a third world country was in 1966 in Jamaica. Ever since, it has been among Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand," said CFG board member Alex Lee.

He said 65 percent of the budget had been met through corporate sponsorships. Malaysia Airines was the largest, contributing air tickets for competing countries worth 50 million ringgit ($20 million).
"We've also got sponsors from Germany such as Siemens and Faber Castell but ironically, we haven't been able to get any from England, where the Commonwealth began," said Hashim.
